title: The Podcast Repurposing Score
subtitle: Find out how much of your podcast you're actually using — and where the gaps are.

questions.text: How clearly defined is the core idea or audience of your podcast?

answers.label: I cover different topics depending on what feels right that week
There's a general theme but it shifts based on guests
I have a focus but don't always stick to it
My podcast has a clear topic and consistent angle
Every episode maps back to one core idea my audience knows me for

answers.label: I haven't started yet
Fewer than 10
More than 100

answers.label: I don't usually think about that after recording
I notice good moments sometimes but rarely act on them
I note the good parts but don't always follow through
I usually have 2 to 3 clear ideas I know I'll repurpose
Before I hit record, I already know what content will come out of it

low.headline: Your episodes are going out, but the engine isn't built yet.
low.text: Before you repurpose anything, you need one idea that runs through everything you record. Not a topic — an angle. What do you want people to know you for after listening to 10 episodes?
steps: Pick one audience and one problem you help them think about differently
Listen back to your last three episodes and write down the single best line from each
Use those lines to test whether you actually have a clear point of view

mid.headline: You have something worth building on — now make it consistent.
mid.text: You've got direction. The question is whether a listener could describe your podcast in one sentence to a friend. If not, your repurposed content will feel scattered too.
steps: Write a one-sentence description of your podcast from a listener's perspective
Check your last five episodes against it — how many actually fit?
Tighten the angle, even if that means narrowing it

high.headline: Strong foundation. This is where the engine runs.
high.text: When your podcast has a clear perspective, every episode becomes source material. You're not just making content — you're building a body of work that compounds over time.
steps: Document your core angle so every future episode connects back to it
Treat your episode archive as a library — the best ideas are already recorded
Start mapping which old episodes deserve a second run as LinkedIn content

questions.text: How many pieces of LinkedIn content do you typically create from one episode?

answers.label: Just the episode link, if that
One or two posts, when I remember
Two to four posts from most episodes
Five or more posts from each episode
I batch-repurpose and one episode runs across weeks of content

questions.text: How long does it take you to turn one episode into a LinkedIn post?

answers.label: A few hours of re-listening and rewriting
About an hour to get something usable
30 to 45 minutes with some structure
Under 20 minutes with a clear process
Under 10 minutes — I have a system for this

questions.text: How far ahead is your LinkedIn content planned from your podcast material?

answers.label: I post when I remember — no real planning
A few days at most
About one week ahead

questions.text: How many podcast episodes do you publish per month?
questions.hint: Include all episodes, solo or with guests

questions.text: How many LinkedIn posts per week come directly from your podcast content?
questions.hint: Count clips, quotes, written posts, and threads

low.headline: You're leaving most of your podcast on the table.
low.text: Every episode you record has at least five LinkedIn posts in it. If you're only sharing the link, you're doing the hard part — the conversation — and skipping the part that builds your audience.
steps: Pick one episode and pull out three moments worth writing about
Start with a quote, a question your guest asked, or a point you disagreed with
Post one of those this week before you record anything new

mid.headline: You're repurposing, but the system isn't repeatable yet.
mid.text: You're getting something out of each episode, which is more than most podcasters do. The gap is in the process — when repurposing takes effort, you do less of it. Make it automatic.
steps: Create a simple template: one quote, one insight, one question from every episode
Batch your repurposing — do three episodes in one sitting, not one at a time
Queue content from your last five episodes before you record the next one

high.headline: Your repurposing is working. Now make it run faster.
high.text: You're getting real mileage from your episodes. The move now is to systematize what's working so you spend less time on process and more time on the ideas.
steps: Document your current process so it holds up even when you're busy
Look at your highest-performing posts and reverse-engineer what made them land
Test AI tools to accelerate first drafts — keep the final call yourself

questions.text: When you sit down to write a LinkedIn post, what usually happens?

answers.label: I write, delete, and rewrite until I give up
I finish a draft but usually don't hit post
I finish most posts but they take longer than they should
I write and post without much friction most of the time
I have a clear starting point every time — the post is done fast

questions.text: How often do you tell yourself you'll post tomorrow and then don't?

answers.label: Most times I sit down to write
Often — probably a few times a week
Sometimes, when I'm stuck on a specific piece
Rarely — I usually follow through
Almost never — my podcast gives me content to pull from anytime

questions.text: When you haven't posted on LinkedIn in a while, how does starting again feel?

answers.label: Like I have to rebuild from scratch
Heavy — like I need to explain or justify the gap
A bit awkward but I push through
Fine — I just pick up where I left off
Easy — my episode backlog means I always have something ready

low.headline: You're in the draft-delete-rewrite loop. That's not burnout — it's pressure.
low.text: The problem isn't content. It's that every post feels like a test. When posting feels like performance, you second-guess everything. One clear idea, posted and moved on from, is worth more than ten drafts that never ship.
steps: Write your next post in under 10 minutes — set a timer
One idea, three to five sentences, post it, don't go back and edit
Your podcast already gave you the idea — stop trying to make it better than the conversation was

mid.headline: You're posting, but the friction is still costing you.
mid.text: You're getting through it, but the pressure is there. The goal isn't to love writing — it's to remove the friction so posting becomes as natural as hitting record.
steps: Find the point in your process where you stall and cut it
Start every post from a real moment in an episode — never from a blank page
Set a rule: if you've spent more than 15 minutes on a post, publish what you have

high.headline: You've broken the pressure loop. This is the gear most people never reach.
high.text: When posting stops feeling heavy, you start to compound. Your backlog grows, your ideas stay fresh, and you're not burning energy on friction. Protect this habit — it's rare.
steps: Don't go more than a week without posting something from your podcast
Share what your process actually looks like — that's a post worth writing
If the pressure ever creeps back, go back to basics: one idea, one post, done

questions.text: How do you currently use AI in your podcast content process?

answers.label: I don't use AI in my content work
I use it to write posts and share them mostly as-is
I use it to clean up or edit my drafts
I use it to generate options I then choose from
I use it to explore directions while keeping the final call myself

questions.text: When AI gives you a draft or suggestion for your content, what do you do with it?

answers.label: I post it with minor edits
I rewrite sections to sound more like me
I use the structure but rewrite most of the words
I treat it as a starting point and usually go a different direction
I compare versions and then make the creative decision myself

questions.text: How well does AI-assisted content currently sound like you?

answers.label: It sounds like a bot wrote it
Close but it doesn't capture my voice
Decent — I can edit it into shape
Sounds like me with a few tweaks
I've trained it on enough of my material that it's a reliable starting point

low.headline: You're not using AI yet — or it's not sounding like you.
low.text: AI is most useful when it gives you directions to explore, not when it makes the decision for you. If you haven't found a workflow where it sounds like you, you haven't found the right one yet.
steps: Feed AI a transcript from your own episode and ask for five different angles on one quote
Don't publish the output — compare the versions and write the one that fits your voice
Start with structure: use AI for the skeleton, write the sentences yourself

mid.headline: You're using AI, but it's still doing more than it should.
mid.text: The goal isn't faster posts. It's more directions to explore, faster. When AI makes the creative call, your content sounds like everyone else's. When you make the call with AI's options in front of you, it sounds like you.
steps: Shift from 'write me a post' to 'give me four different angles on this quote'
Add one rewrite pass where you replace any line that doesn't sound like you
Test it: would your regular listeners recognize this as yours?

high.headline: You've figured out how to use AI as an exploration tool, not a replacement.
high.text: This is the right relationship with the tool. You're getting more directions to explore without losing the creative call. Most people either avoid AI or hand it too much. You've found the middle.
steps: Document the prompts that work so you can repeat them
Use AI to surface angles in old episodes you haven't repurposed yet
Keep the final edit as yours — that's what makes your content yours
